Input: Is NATO afraid of Vladimir Putin? On this photo you see how 10 years ago, in the early hours of the morning on July 2014, Girkin’s military gang entered the peaceful, calm and wealthy Ukrainian city of Donetsk, turning life there into hell. Putin’s propaganda said they were “Donetsk miners and tractor drivers” who suddenly decided they needed independence. Answering the question why Girkin’s column was not destroyed, advisor to Ukraine’s minister of internal affairs Anton Gerashchenko explained in his 2016 interview that “someone at the very top was simply afraid to make the difficult decision to shoot at the column”. The officials were too afraid of numerous victims. As the result of this timidness, Ukraine now has a real war and tens of thousands of victims. NATO isn’t afraid of Vladimir Putin — it’s afraid of numerous victims.

How would the provision of Patriot air defence systems affect the situation in the city of Kharkiv? More than 10% of the population of Kharkiv (160,000 people) have lost their homes, 5 thousand buildings suffered damages or have been destroyed by the Russian artillery, missiles and bombs. If Kharkiv had effective air defence systems like Patriots, with sufficient munitions for them, this wouldn’t have happened. The White House administration has finally approved the use of American air defence systems to shoot down Russian planes over the Russian territory — that’s where they drop their guided bombs, which fall on Kharkiv and nearby towns. The new direction on the use of the U.S. weapons will allow Ukraine to employ American weapons to intercept Russian missiles that are targeting Kharkiv, and to attack concentrations of Russian troops just over the border in the vicinity of the city. This will allow for Ukraine to aim for high value targets such as command and control centers, artillery, logistics and air defence units that are located on Russian territory near Kharkiv and concentrating or rehearsing future operations against Ukraine. Russian propagandists must be devastated. No instruction manuals have been received from the AP (administration of the president) as yet, so they are keeping num about it.

What will happen to economics in Russia? “Always low prices” alcohol store a year ago, in June 2023, and now, in June 2024: that’s the price for cheap beer made in Belgium and Germany. Price rise of over 35%. Russian people, most of whom buy the cheapest available goods (regardless of the quality), struggle to purchase food and drinks they used to be able to afford. After mass-market foreign clothing brands like “H&M” left Russia, local clothing chains raised their prices by 50–100% — for the same quality clothing as they were selling before. The difference in prices “before the war” and now is staggering for residents of Rostov, who try to save not only on entertainment and clothing, or occasional coffees in a cafe, but also on basic essentials like purchasing store-made baby food — there is simply no money in a family budget left for that in a family of 3, with father’s solo income of 50,000 rub. per month ($500). In Russia, a monthly salary of USD $2000-3000 is considered “high” — only 3% of the population earn such money. People who earn $2,000 per month are viewed in Russia as “rich”. Russia is a poor country and the war will ruin it completely.

Does Russia have any Red Dawn type movies showing an American invasion? Russians are too scared to make movies about an American invasion. In Russian movies, Americans aren’t shown as a fierce and mighty enemy — they are shown as goofy halfwits. This week, Russian TNT channel presented an upcoming series about the adventures of Joe Biden in Russia. It will be a comedy about POTUS flying to Russia incognito to understand why sanctions are not working. According to the script, the American president loses his documents, lives in a minuscule apartment, erected in a hurry during Khrushchev times, works as an English teacher and befriends a “true Russian patriot.” The series, titled “Goodbye,” will be a “kind, true-to-life, funny story,” promises actor Dmitry Dyuzhev, who is playing Joe Biden. Dyuzhev previously played a pregnant man in one of his films. In the real world of politics, "Sleepy Joe" outplayed Putin 50:0. And now, in retaliation, the Russian TV is going to mock the US president. The Russian industry of movie-making is dead. Anyone who refuses to see the reality through Putin's eyes has simply left the country. The rest resigned to filming propaganda on orders of ideologists from the presidential administration. But even in propaganda, the idea of America invading Russia (or anyone invading Russia, for that matter) is too unthinkable for Putin’s underlings. There are simply no movies like that. The only movies about a foreign invasion are from WW2 times or some other old history tales.

What will happen if Russia runs out of manpower for the military? August 2024: Russian soldiers surrender en masse in the Kursk region of Russia, overpowered and outnumbered by the Ukrainian forces in their own territory. How the tables have turned: The photos of the annihilated Russian column that was bringing soldiers to the front in the Kursk region are all over the Russian social networks. The Russian correspondents first showed the column moving through the Kursk region, and then other Russians filmed it burning and the aftermath of the attack. The FSB arrested a man who filmed the burning trucks and made him confess that he was doing it on orders of the Ukrainians. Someone has to be blamed for the major security screw up! And another Russian propagandist from the military channel ‘Zvezda’ (‘Star’) was proudly filming another Russian column going through the Kursk region yesterday — already after the previous column got burned. Learning from their mistakes is for the wimps. Russian propaganda professionals are trained in bragging and boasting, not tactical stealth. There are basically no professionally trained junior army officers with combat experience left in Russia — almost all of them are dead by now. That’s why the screwups like the one with the burned column become possible — no one learned the instructions clearly stating that when resting, soldiers need to spread and hide, as opposed to stopping on the side of the road with no gaps between the vehicles, with the personnel remaining in the trucks. It looks more likely with every day that Russia will have to do another mass mobilization, to compensate for the terrible losses at the front. In order to achieve the "goals of the SMO" as Putin formulated them, the Russian army would need to call up another 3-4 million men — at least 1.5 million of them would end up killed or maimed, until it becomes obvious to everyone in Russia that achieving Putin’s stated goals is simply impossible. Despite Kremlin’s constantly raising payouts for signing up to go to the war, the number of Russian “volunteers” has dropped sharply — there are (almost) no fools left to die for money — even rather large sums of money (by the Russian standards). By 2024, Ukraine has more soldiers to fight off Russia than Russia has “contractors” who agreed to go to another country and become murderers, in hopes to pay off their debts. The Russian propagandists promote the idea that the Ukrainian army will run out of people faster because the Ukrainian population is smaller. It is true, the Ukrainian population is smaller — but that’s not all the truth: the attacking army needs to have a multifold numerical advantage to succeed. But the Russian army has no such advantage. On top of that, Russia is undoubtedly behind the Ukrainian army in technological terms. Even if Russia could manage to mobilize and equip 3–4 million soldiers, they still wouldn’t be able to close the technological gap. When Russia attacked Ukraine in February 2022, they had an enormous advantage in terms of manpower and weapons — but the balance has been slowly shifting to the other side. By now, Ukraine has the advantage of the modern technology and weapons, as well as the backing of the economies producing over 50% of the global GDP. Putin is not only running out of manpower, but also out of stockpiles of the Soviet weapons and money to finance the military production and the army. The Ukrainian incursion in the Kursk region further destabilizes the whole system. Putin has no time to mobilize the manpower. It’s not impossible that the whole Russian front in Ukraine might collapse. Follow me for more updates!
Will Putin attack NATO? Putin said on June 5, 2024, at St. Petersburg’s economic forum: Thank you, Mr. Putin. Now everyone understands.

What do you make of the fact that Paul Whelan was left out of the prisoner exchange between the US and Russia? In December 2022, Paul Whelan wasn’t part of a prisoner exchange between Russia and the U.S. — instead, American basketball player Brittney Greener was traded for Russian arms dealer Victor Bout. Since then, there weren’t exchanges that were made public. Exchanges are never straightforward and who gets back is determined not only by what one side desires but also whom the opposition is prepared to exchange. Victor Bout, Brittney Griner. Putin managed to get his “merchant of death” Bout back, releasing an American hostage Griner who was arrested in Russia for carrying vaporizer cartridges containing less than a gram of hash oil. Russia accused her in possession of illegal drugs and sentenced for 9 years of prison. While possessing marijuana is illegal in Russia, the whole arrest and sentencing of Griner were handled with such media frenzy and promotion by Russian propagandists and the Kremlin bots online that it looked like a special operation to pressure the American side to release a well-connected arms dealer — by the end of 2022, Putin desperately needed someone experienced in that particular sector. Why Paul Whelan wasn’t exchanged at the time was asked by many, and the answer is that maybe Russia wanted someone else in exchange to Whelan whom the FSB insists was a real spy. Security professional Paul Whelan was arrested in Moscow in 2018 and accused of being a spy. Whelan said he had been in Russia for a friend's wedding. Before 2008, Whelan served as a Marine, and after his discharge was working as a security chief for a commercial organization. He visited Russia several times before and the wedding he was planning to attend was of a fellow marine. Whelan says he was given the hard drive by a Russian friend in what he now he now believes was a “sting operation” — Russia accused the drive contained some classified intel and sentenced him to 16 years imprisonment. This week, after several Russian political prisoners disappeared from their prisons in Russia, it was discovered that Paul Whelan is also missing. So are Putin’s critics journalist Maria Ponomarenko and an opposition politician Vladimir Kara-Murza. More confirmations are coming from Russia that a big prisoner exchange deal is in the works. Maybe this time Paul Whelan will also be released.

How is the Russian economy doing? What kind of data has its economy produced in recent months, positive or negative? From January 2020 to May 2024, inflation in Russia is double the G7 average. Russia’s central bank had to raise its base interest rate from 7.5% in June 2023 to 16% in June 2024 — and in July 2024, it was increased by 200 basis points at once — to 18% per annum. So, Russia’s base interest rate is 3% higher than in Afghanistan. There are no plans to reduce the key rate this year, stated Elvira Nabiullina, head of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation. She added that the rate will remain high for a long time, and an additional increase is possible. Thank the glorious leader Vladimir Putin for that. Meanwhile, a Russian economist who was explaining how badly Russia was doing just “accidentally fell out of a window”. Another unfortunate accident amidst the epidemic of high-rise falls of state execs in the Russian capital. Russia is doing just fine — even great, insisted Vladimir Putin in his recent speech in the Kremlin, promising that the economy of the occupied Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Donetsk and Luhansk regions will be by 2030 on the level of “the rest of Russia”. (Video in the comments below.) If anyone saw the devastation of “the rest of Russia”, this certainly sounds like a threat rather than an optimistic forecast. And it’s highly doubtful that Russia is capable to quickly bring back to life the destroyed Ukrainian cities. Mariupol, Bakhmut, Avdeevka, Marinka — these Ukrainian cities had their own thriving identities before the war — Russia put on them the mangled masks of the “Russian world.” The ruins are visible on Google Planet, from satellites. In the past weeks, Russia got hit by rolling blackouts — in Krasnodar region, people went to the streets to protest, after not having power and water for several days — the water supply was switched off because there was no power. There are rumors of an accident at a nuclear power station near Rostov, and as a result, insufficient power produced to supply the nearby regions. The “new regions” — how Putin calls the occupied Ukrainian territories — are getting the power from Russia; before the occupation, they were getting the electricity from Ukraine. The Russian grid hadn’t been maintained and repaired properly due to the lack of funds (the money is spent on the war in Ukraine) and western sanctions (parts aren’t easily accessible — and Russia doesn’t make them). Russia is stuck in Ukraine and the money is disappearing in the black hole of the war, with nothing but ruined cities to show for that. And these ruined cities will require an enormous investment to bring them back to life — and who’s going to invest in a territory that’s occupied and can change its citizenship or be bombed to ruins tomorrow? “Russians will have many more troubles because the country is worn out. It was necessary to close Russia down for the major renovation for about 10 years. Then it would’ve been possible to live through the 21st century normally. Instead of that, the country was sent to war,” says Igor Lipsits, a prominent Russian economist and founder of the Higher School of Economics in Moscow, who was forced to emigrate because of his critical stance. The Russian economy is in a state of flux. The western sanctions suffocate it slowly but surely — and this is why Putin keeps demanding the lifting of western sanctions as a condition of a “peace agreement”. Because Russia is screwed unless the sanctions are lifted — no matter what is the situation on the ground in Ukraine. There is really no good scenario for the Russian economy — its down spiral is irreversible at this point. It’s like a worn off car — it requires a complete rebuild to operate properly again.

What is happening in the Kursk region of Russia? In the Kursk region of Russia, which Ukrainian army invaded on August 6, things are moving fast. Ukraine already controls 100 settlements and the territory of 1,300 km², reported commander-in-chief Syrskyi. Time to let Ukraine take Russia! Russian military bloggers say that Ukrainian forces broke through defenses in Belgorod region — that’s the second Russian region getting invaded. Meanwhile, Russian volunteers who arrived to Kursk region with “humanitarian aid” for the Russian army (food, water, socks and jocks for soldiers, because the Russian army doesn’t provide for its troops — officers steal all the money) — so, these “volunteers” complain about traffic police cameras, which continue to send them tickets for speeding — while they are driving over the speed limits to avoid drones or shelling. The traffic police office responded that “war is war, but a violation is a violation” and fines that have already been issued in the system can only be challenged in court. You know, in Russia the law is the law! (Unless, of course, you are above the law, in which case you can break any laws you want.) I suppose, the Ukrainian tanks must have scored hundreds of fines for illegal parking. The new map of Eastern Europe has just been leaked on Telegram. On 24 February 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, the world was discussing how long Ukraine would be able to withstand against Russia — 2 days, 3 days, a week? Not many gave Ukraine more than 2 weeks. On August 6, 2024, when Ukraine invaded the Kursk region of Russia, Vladimir Putin ordered “to squeeze the enemy out”. On day 3, the chief of Russian general staff Gerasimov reported to Putin that the enemy had been repelled and destroyed. That was more than 3 weeks ago. Ukrainians are still in the Kursk region and keep increasing their stronghold. And now , Russians are told by their TV channels that "The incursion into Kursk region by the Ukrainians is beneficial to Russia, because it closes the conversations about negotiations with Ukraine.” Putin hopes that “the situation” in the Kursk region will somehow sort itself out, so he tries not to make a big deal about “mighty Russia” getting invaded by a “little, insignificant Ukraine.” Being invaded by a foreign power is Russia’s “new normal”.

How does the arrest of Laurent Vinatier, a French researcher who was charged with violating the "foreign agents" law in Russia, affect international relations? Laurent Vinatier, a French researcher who was charged with violating the "foreign agents" law, was arrested in Russia and sent to pre-trial detention on June 7, 2024. Yesterday, he appeared in a Moscow court for a hearing, asking to be allowed to stay under house arrest, but his request was denied by the judge. Vinatier seemed a shadow of his confident self from a month ago. He appeared at the hearing via a video link. The French consul general in Moscow was present at the hearing. Vinatier was arrested immediately after the French president Macron said that France would send troops to Ukraine, in the worst Russia’s traditions of “hostage diplomacy”. About the same time 26-year-old native of Donbas with dual Russian and Ukrainian citizenship was detained in France on suspicion of preparing a terrorist attack. At the very first hearing on June 7 that sent him to jail on accusations of failing to register as a “foreign agent”, Vinatier was demonstratively thrown in a cage in the courtroom. At the hearing on July 4, the prosecution alleged that Vinatier was guilty of collecting military information. The prosecution didn’t disclose what information Vinatier shouldn’t be privy to, but stated that it "could be used against state security." The accusation of not registering as a “foreign agent” — which Vinatier said he wasn’t aware he was required to do — is usually reserved for Russian citizens who are financed by foreign entities and involved in political activities. But recent changes to the law require anyone who “collects information on military issues” to register as a “foreign agent”. The 48-year-old Frenchman is an adviser with the Geneva-based ‘Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue’, a Swiss conflict mediation organization, and a long-time researcher of Russia and other post-Soviet countries. Russia has been using its "foreign agent" laws to jail domestic critics for a long time, and now the regime is doing it to foreign citizens as well. On June 21, 2024, Vinatier was included in the Russian register of “foreign agents”. Vinatier attended the court hearing on July 4 via a video link from the detention centre — he wasn’t brought to the court. The judge extended his detention until August 5. Any foreign citizen in Russia is a potential hostage and an instrument of exerting pressure on democratically elected governments, especially during elections. Hostages are also used as leverage in negotiations. Kremlin bots are pushing such topics in social media to stir emotions and cause division. In case of Vinatier, Kremlin bots are already driving the story to notoriety. Under the current accusation, Vinatier can be imprisoned for up to 5 years.

Just take it in: 18% base rate! According to Nabiullina, that was required “to stop the economy from overheating.” The truth is, the war that Putin refuses to stop is killing the Russian economy. Main points from Nabiullina’s briefing: In her own words: Meanwhile, the regular Russians live their regular lives. One thing that Putin makes sure doesn’t change is the cost of cheap alcohol — vodka and beer. In the online shop in Russia, vodka is sold from 335 rub. for 0.5 liter bottle — that’s about USD $3.50 (yes, less than $4). That’s the main factor behind Russians’ infamous capacity to endure hardships. Cheap alcohol for the masses. It helps to keep the population under control, but obedient drunks cannot build a strong economy. It will be always substandard.

Do you think Russia will ever hand over Sergei K. Shoigu and Gen. Valery V. Gerasimov to the International Criminal Court? To celebrate 1-year anniversary of Prigozhin’s rebellion, The Hague International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Sergei Shoigu, former minister of defence of Russia, and Valery Gerasimov, Chief of General Staff. Now, not only Putin and children’s ombudsman Maria Lvova-Belova are on the list of international war criminals, but the top guys who commanded the troops to attack Ukraine, are being wanted in Hague for shelling civilians. Sergei Shoigu was removed from his job of the minister of defence in May 2024, and given the nominal position the secretary of Russia’s security council; Valery Gerasimov remains the chief of general staff. Handing war criminals to prosecution is a requirement of Ukraine’s Peace Plan. This will be surely a requirement to lift western sanctions from Russia, which became the most sanctioned country in the world after its treacherous attack on Ukraine in February 2022, surpassing Iran and North Korea. And this is why, after Putin’s sudden death, Russia will gleefully hand all the war criminals to Hague, to get rid of the sanctions. Meanwhile, in Makhachkala, Dagestan, masked militants with guns are again walking in the streets. Residents shared home videos from Korkmasova Street: armed police officers take positions, there are shootouts in streets. In Makhachkala, security forces blocked off a square in the city center. (Video in the comments below.) After June 23 attacks on churches and synagogues, Dagestan’s authorities accused (surprise, surprise) America in organizing the attacks, “to split the unity of the Russian people”. Today, there is more unrest — and the attackers are well-equipped. There were expectations that Caucasus would inflame amidst Russia’s war in Ukraine, and it’s not the first time that Dagestan is in the news because of unrest since February 2022. But previous mass protests in Dagestan didn’t involve armed militants and shootouts with the police. Could these be the groups that complete what Yevgeny Prigozhin started on June 23, 2023, and march all the way to Moscow?

Has Quora been targeted by Putin trolls? So many questions lately are just risible idiotic nonsense. That’s what we think Russian troll farms look like. And that’s what they actually look like: A video depicting the work of a “social media promotion agency” from Vietnam was leaked online (video in the comments below) — and it’s not the only one, you can be sure about it. Russian, Chinese and even North Korean and Iranian state propaganda departments are outsourcing their “social media promotion” to Asian companies located in Vietnam, Indonesia, India, and Philippines. Special programs are creating thousands of social media accounts that spew nearly identical comments, accompanied by nearly identical photos and videos, but which are slightly modified by AI to appear different to social media algorithms. Russia, China and Iran use these troll factories to promote their narratives, as well as to divide westerners. The online aggravation and arguments are usually result of the bots’ activities. It is these troll accounts that you are arguing with online. Their goal is to cause heated emotions and spread hatred, in the best traditions of “divide and conquer”. They aim to break our democratic political systems from the inside, make us fight between ourselves, rather than stand united against totalitarian dictatorships — because totalitarian regimes cannot win if we are united. The same tools are used by foreign propaganda outlets on Quora to ask questions and comment on answers. No longer they have to have a human typing questions by hand — AI tools generate dozens of variations of the same question that are asked by dozens of different accounts, making it harder to detect. And they are using bot accounts, created in 2014 onwards, to upvote and downvote certain answers. It’s a big business for Internet troll farms right now. We are under a massive attack by foreign forces — every single one of us. Stand strong.

Why do you think Putin decided to kill dozens of babies in a Kiev children's hospital on the very day that Russians celebrate "Family Day"? Putin decided to kill dozens of babies in a Kiev children's hospital on the very day that Russians celebrate “the Day of Family, Love and Loyalty" to demonstrate to his subjects: your family can live in peace only if you are loyal to Putin and plead to love Russia. And if you don’t want to see Putin as your ruler and don’t plead to love Russia, then your kids and your family will be killed by Russian missiles. That’s a message not just to Ukraine — it’s the message to the whole of Europe. Kyiv, July 8, 2024. A first responder at the site of a strike at the children’s hospital. Not just 1 but 3 Ukraine’s hospitals were targeted in yesterday’s strike: after hitting Ukraine's largest children's hospital "Okhmatdyt", Russia hit a maternity hospital in Kyiv where mothers come to give birth. Another hospital was hit in the city of Kryvyi Rih. The missile strike was absolutely deliberate, stated Mykhailo Podolyak, advisor to the office of president of Ukraine: children's hospital "Okhmatdyt" was hit with Kh-101 class missile. Podolyak spelled out 3 “unconditional conclusions” in connection with the deliberate missile strike on Ukraine's largest children's hospital: That’s Putin’s way to assert his geopolitical paradigm in his unrelenting drive to destroy the rules-based world order. And he’s not just talking about it — he’s demonstrating it in the most blatant and abhorrent way.

In Russia, did the video of the effeminate Russian soldiers surrendering to the manly Ukraine army make them embarrassed? TAP ON PHOTO TO VIEW. Young Russian conscripts saved by the Ukrainian army from certain death — Putin’s goons sent them to fight hardened Ukrainian fighters, but the kids were so scared, they surrendered. Russia has a 1-year compulsory military service that ever male must go through at the age of 18. Those who study at universities get to finish their studies first, before they are drafted. So, if you have graduated from the high school and didn’t get into college, you are immediately drafted into the army. Compulsory draftees aren’t supposed to be used in combat in the war, but you know, it’s Russia. The Russian generals decided it’s time to send everyone they have to the slaughter, to stop the Ukrainian incursion in the Kursk region — and another one, rumored to soon be incursion in the Belgorod region. In St. Petersburg, about 500 “refuseniks” were sent to the Kursk region. They included sick, mentally unwell, old, and “peaceniks”. Some of the captured Russian conscripts even tried to blow themselves up with a grenade — but failed, because of lack of experience. They say that the commanders brainwash them to blow themselves up to avoid being taken captive — the commanders tells them that otherwise, they would face incredible torture in the Ukrainian captivity. (Video in the comments below.) The unsuccessful grenade blower (who was hurt but not gravely) was shocked at how kindly he was treated by the Ukrainians — better than by their own commanders. These testimonies will be certainly of interest to the Human Rights commission of the UN and prosecutors of the Russian war crimes. The number and quality of those captured by the Ukrainian army in the Kursk region is so great (even some Kadyrov guys were taken captive, although Kadyrovets are given the order not to surrender — so they usually run away in case of any danger), that Russians even asked for a prisoner swap — apparently, for the first time during the war. This was reported by Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets. But if you were watching the Russian TV, you’d never hear about 2,000 Russians soldiers taken captive within 8 days — according to the Russian TV, things are going great in the Kursk region, Ukrainians are being defeated, “the situation has been stabilized”, and Russia is victorious, as always. As the war has been progressing through the last 2.5 years, Russians are getting more and more victorious — and the victories are happening closer and closer to Moscow. We soon might hear about new Russian victories in Belgorod and Bryansk regions.

What role did the European Union play in the collapse of the Soviet Union, besides economic factors? The Maastricht Treaty that laid down the foundation for the European Union was signed in 1992 and went into effect in 1993. The Belovezha Accords that resulted in dissolution of the Soviet Union were signed in 1991. The desire of the first Russia’s president Boris Yeltsin to take full control of the whole of Russia, without having to report to the Union state and the USSR president Gorbachev, was the main driver of that move. 3 presidents — of Belarus, Russia and Ukraine — signed the Belovezha accords on December 8, 1991. They actually were supposed to negotiate a new Confederation deal between the republics, to reenergize the Soviet Union, but the 3 presidents chose to destroy it instead. The European Union had nothing to do with it. It was pure greed and lust for power of the first elected leader of Russia.

Why is Russian propaganda spreading like wildfire around the world? AI-driven fake social media accounts impersonating Americans are run by Russian bot farms — the FBI has a proof. The U.S. Justice Department shot down a Russian bot farm, seized 2 domain names and convinced X-Twitter to suspend 968 social media accounts used by Russia to create disinformation campaigns in the United States and abroad. The fictitious social media profiles claiming to be Americans promoted Russian state propaganda. The following are examples of Russian-government narratives that the bot farm posted on X-Twitter in October-November 2023: To register the fictitious social media accounts, the bot farm used private email servers of the 2 domain names seized by the FBI. (An owner of a domain name can create unlimited email addresses for that domain name.) “The FSB’s use of U.S.-based domain names, which the software used to register the bots, violates the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. In addition, the accompanying payments for that infrastructure violate federal money laundering laws,” the FBI press release states. So, the American FBI is accusing the Russian FSB not in interfering with the American politics, but in violating the money laundering laws. Awesome job! Hard to say why this ”bot farm bust” was important to make public right now — obviously, we all know about Kremlin bots and see their accounts spitting Chat-GPT instructions in Russian when the FSB cards on file get cut off due to sanctions or another issue (I reported on that before). Not only we know about Kremlin bots using AI and intuitively figured it out long ago, but Margarita Simonyan herself blabbed about it in her February 2024 interview to a Russian TV program “Life and Destiny” (“Zhizn i Sudba”): she precisely explained how they create multiple accounts in social networks and “the CIA bans them”, but as they ban some profiles, RT keeps creating even more. By the looks of it, after the death of Yevgeny Prigozhin in August 2023, his bot farms have been transferred into ‘Russia Today’ department and given an AI-powered makeover. Now, only another 29-million-something of these accounts are left to ban.

Was Stalin really that bad, or was he a victim of propaganda? In 1930s, young Mikhail Sholokhov was already a known author in the USSR for his book “Tales of the Don” (1925), depicting his personal experiences during the WWI, the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 and the Civil War. When Stalin’s attack on peasants with the goal of shoveling them into “collective farms” began, Sholokhov lived in the village of Veshenskaya, Rostov region, and could see what was happening with the people. Witnessing the deaths and suffering of peasants, Sholokhov wrote 4 letters to Stalin in hopes of saving people. April 20, 1932: “I saw something that cannot be forgotten till my last days: at night, in the Volokhovsky village of the Lebyazhensky collective farm, in the fierce wind, in the freezing cold, when even dogs were hiding from the frosty weather, families of peasants who were thrown out of their houses had been burning fires in the alleys and sitting near the flames. Children were wrapped in rags and laid on the bare ground, thawed by the fire. A continuous children’s cry stood over the alleys. Why are people being tortured like that? In the Bazkovsky collective farm, a woman with a baby was evicted from her home. She was walking around the village all night, asking to be allowed to warm up with her child. Nobody let her in, fearing that if they do, they themselves would be evicted. By morning, the child froze to death in his mother's arms...” Stalin replied that Sholokhov simply lacked the class consciousness. Yes, Stalin was absolutely evil. It’s not just “propaganda”.

What are some significantly awesome 'Meanwhile in Russia' photos? If you are lucky of course and your commander reports you dead — or you may end up as “missing” or an unidentified body in an overfilled morgue. Bodies of Russian soldiers that were killed on August 7 are yet to be identified from 6 days ago. Because of maxing out on capacity, bodies from Kursk are no longer being taken to Rostov. Russian channels insist that Ukrainians are already retreating. Judging by the maps, towards Moscow.

What the hell is going on in Russia? Is it the case that Medvedev drinks a lot? Does the world know the Kursk offensive was nothing more than a PR stunt by Ukraine, in order to manufacture some type of hope for more funding? “Ukrainian offensive in Kursk is just a PR stunt” was the first stage of denial for Putin’s propagandists. After that, they began reporting about “destroyed enemy forces” and “the situation has been stabilized.” For over 10 days since August 6, Ukraine keeps advancing and enlarging the area under control. Yesterday, a key bridge over the Seim River in Glushkovo was destroyed in a series of ATACMS strikes, Now, Russian reinforcements from a huge area in Kursk region are essentially cut off. Reportedly, 700 Russian soldiers are left stranded with no supplies The area under control of the Ukrainian armed forces keeps growing daily. It’s expected to continue. With the destruction of the bridge, the whole south-western part of Kursk region (over 50 settlements) is cut off from the rest of Russia. The Ukrainian forces are now targeting another of bridge in the village of Zvannoye, one of the 2 smaller bridges that are still operational. If all bridges are destroyed, further 700km² would fall under Ukraine’s control, in addition to the 1,100km² already controlled by Ukraine. If Ukraine keeps blowing up bridges and seizing territories west of the river, the Ukrainian Armed Forces will control 3-4 thousand square kilometers, full of with underground bunkers and storages, build by Russians as fortifications. In early 1990s, the KGB seized a similar territory in Moldova and established so-called Transnistria Republic. Russia still controls this territory and uses it to create problems for Moldova. Meanwhile, some Russian propagandists warn that squeezing out the Ukrainian forces from Kursk can “take months” — and other go as far as suggesting that Russia can lose this war. Ukraine’s Kursk offensive has blown a giant hole in the tale that “Russia is keeping its best forces in reserve”. No, they don’t: they are ”all in” in Ukraine — and are now trying to plug the hole with fresh conscripts serving compulsory 1-year service, unable to find any trained troops or “contractors” hired specifically for the Ukrainian war. Makes you think, right?

Did Ukraine just test its first ballistic missile? Ukraine had the capability to build ballistic missiles since the times of the USSR, but after signing the Budapest memorandum in 1994, Ukraine had to dispose of its arsenal of carriers of strategic nuclear warheads. Ukraine also surrendered to Russia many missiles that Putin’s army used in attacks since February 2022. So, when president Zelenskyy announced on August 27, 2024, that Ukraine has successfully tested its new ballistic missile, it was something that many analysts expected for a long time. Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon (left), who was a friend of former Ukrainian president Leonid Kuchma (right) described their conversation in 2006 when Kuchma told him that Ukraine had both the capability and expertise to build ballistic missiles. Kuchma also told Gordon that Ukraine was able to build “as many as necessary” ballistic missiles. Leonid Kuchma knew what he was talking about. He began working on ‘Yuzhmash’ aerospace plant in the Ukrainian city of Dnipropetrovsk in 1960, straight after graduation from a university as an engineer. On ‘Yuzhmash’, Kuchma was working in the design bureau, where the Soviet missile systems were created. Then he moved to the position of technical director of rocket tests at the Baikonur Cosmodrome — the #1 space rocket launching pad of the USSR. During his career, Kuchma worked as a chief of both legendary flagships of the Ukrainian rocket and space industry — ‘Yuzhmash’ aerospace plant and ‘Yuzhnoye’ design bureau. For his contribution to development of rocket engineering, Kuchma was awarded the Lenin Prize in 1979 (12 years before the dissolution of the USSR). After Kuchma became the 2nd president of independent Ukraine, the first Ukrainian satellite "Sich-1" was launched into space (1995). In an interview to BBC in June 2022, Kuchma said that the latest developments of Dnepropetrovsk aerospace engineers included analogues of western weapons that Ukraine had to beg western partners for: for example, missile systems with a range of hundreds of kilometers. So, the appearance of Ukrainian-made ballistic missiles was only a matter of time — and I think Putin knew it, this is why he was in such a hurry to pressure Ukraine to sign a “peace agreement” that would prohibit further development of Ukrainian weapons. But Putin underestimated both Ukraine and the West. And now his strategic loss is obvious to anyone keeping abreast of the latest developments in this war.

How many casualties has Russia suffered? Moscow region increased the one-off payout on signup for the willing cannon fodder for the Ukrainian war — these willing to play the death lottery are now offered 1.9 million ruble (around USD $22,000). In addition, there is the federal payout of 225,000 rub., bringing the total premium to $24,000 per head. The move is caused by plunging numbers of volunteers — and each region must deliver a certain number of soldiers per year, on Putin’s orders. The typical volunteer recruit comes from depressed regional towns of Russia — of which there are tens of thousands. Muscovites live reasonably well, the city life is at full swing, no one is interested in dying to stop mythical Nazis in Ukraine. Thus, raids on migrants to send these with Russian passports to the army, and pressurize illegals to sign the contract under the threat of imprisonment. But that’s still not enough. This is why the Russian state constantly raises the one-off payments for signing the army contract, which make it feasible for poor Russians from regions to travel to Moscow to sign up. Recruiters lie and tell aspiring high-wage-earners that they would be “safeguarding warehouses in the rear” or “digging trenches”. But when they arrive to Ukraine — after a 2-week stunt at a training camp (where most recruits mostly drink and hang out with newly made friends) — they are simply shipped to the front trenches and given a gun, and told to hold positions. Under a heavy fire. And there is no one to complain to. But even with all the tricks and money on offer, Russia can only deliver about 25,000-30,000 new recruits monthly, which isn’t enough to replenish the heavy losses. By the end of July 2024, the losses of the Russian army reached over 570,000 personnel, killed and wounded. Russia’s average daily losses in the last 2 months exceed 1,000 personnel daily. In Kazan, a referral fee of 100,000 ruble ($1,150) is paid to those who bring a friend to the military registration office to sign up for the war in Ukraine. A friend in need is a friend indeed. Other regions are also raising payouts on signup for the war. Russia is struggling to maintain the numbers at the front, and the only thing that worked before to get volunteers — money — is losing its appeal.

What is the likelihood that Putin, Shoigu, and Gerasimov will be arrested? “We hope to see them behind bars,” commented Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky on the decision of The Hague International Criminal Court to issue arrest warrants for Shoigu and Gerasimov — the arrest warrant for Putin was issued in March 2023. Personally, I think that there is a much higher likelihood of Putin’s sudden death, followed by arrests of the Russian generals and top officials. However, the arrest and prosecution of Vladimir Putin and Dmitry Medvedev for the crime of usurping power is what the Congress of Russian deputies in exile demanded. There are dozens of former members of the Russian State Duma that have been forced by Putin’s government to emigrate. The Congress of People's Deputies wants to try Putin and Medvedev in Russia, without them spending years in comfortable European cells, but still in cooperation with the International Criminal Court. Sooner or later, war criminals who started the devastating war in Ukraine will be prosecuted. It may not happen this year or in 2025 — but by 2032, the Russian Federation won’t be the country it is today. It will have a different leader and a different government. Putin’s gang, which crept into power following his appointment as a “successor” by Yeltsin in 1999, will be hunted, arrested and thrown in prison where they belong.

Are there any specific stories within the 100 Ukrainians released from Russian captivity that you found particularly moving? Here is this story that I cried reading. You might cry, too. A guy tells his mother after being released from captivity: “We didn’t believe in the exchange until the very end. Because they deceived us so much, they tormented us... They would take us for executions and for exchanges... And then they would bring us back and laugh at us. And when a soldier came into the bus and said, "You’re home, boys, Glory to Ukraine!" - I just started breathing; I hadn't been breathing, Mom, really. And when we saw people along the road greeting us with flags, flowers, and signs, it felt like a movie, like it wasn’t happening to us. And then, when we finally arrived, the first cigarette, hugs, they gave us a phone, I forgot your number, Mom, can you imagine? But you’re not mad, because how could I forget your number? I repeated it to myself for 2 years. Like you taught me in childhood - "My name is...., I live at..., Mom’s phone number is...." The boys cried, but I didn't. And at the hospital, they gave us clothes and took us to the dining room. And there was food, Mom. There were 3 bowls of different things for each of us. I don’t know, I didn’t eat that much in captivity in a month. And the smell of the soup. My head started spinning. The bowl was so deep, the soup was up to the brim. I was so careful with the spoon, trying not to spill anything, but my hands were shaking, Mom, because I wanted to eat properly, but I also wanted to just grab the bowl and drink it all. And my hands were shaking. And oh, how much I wanted to eat, you can’t imagine. And I was so careful, trying to be proper... A lady walked around, refilling everything for us, she came up to me, hugged me, stroked my head like Grandma used to, kissed me on the temple - "Eat, dear, I’ll bring more," she said. And that’s when I cried. I ate and cried, afraid to look up because I felt ashamed. And then I looked around, and almost all of us were like that - eating and crying. And the soup, Mom, I’ve never had anything tastier in my life. You’re not upset, are you, Mom?”

Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem? A Russian deserter who was tricked to sign up for the war told ‘The Insider’ how he was nearly killed by his own Russian troops at the front, next to a pit with 20–30 bodies. He was badly wounded when his commander sent him to pick some vodka, and nearly bled out with no assistance. It was after this experience that he decided to run off. Anton (not his real name) had no intention of joining the army whatsoever. But in the fall of 2023, he went out to a shop, and a police patrol stopped him to check his documents. Anton didn’t have his ID with him and the cops took him to the police station. They put his data into a computer and told him he had an outstanding mobilization summons and would be going to the front in 3 days. They threatened that he would have huge problems for trying to skip mobilization — but there could be a way around: he could go to the enlistment office and ask to sign the contract voluntarily. The cops told him that if he signed the contract (as opposed to being mobilized), he would be able to pick an “easy” job, like helping out in a hospital. Anton came home horrified. The idea of improving his odds to get an “easy” military job as opposed to being sent to the front as mobilized seemed reasonable. He decided that if he anyway would be mobilized, he’d better become a contractor. He signed the contract on Saturday, and on Tuesday he was already sent to a unit. And — surprise, surprise! — he was sent to an assault company. A week later he was already at the front line. That was a shock for Anton: “A week ago I was sitting at home, watching videos, working, leading a normal life, and now I'm at the trenches in Ukraine.” It didn’t take long at the front for commanders to start sending people to assaults. His unit’s goal was to take a position at the edge of a village. But to get there, the soldiers had to run over 500 meters of an open space. From the Ukrainian side, that open space was controlled by a machine gun that was able to take out up to 100 people at once. The only cover a group could take was a damaged tank stranded in the middle. The commander told the assault teams to take cover and dig an outpost near the tank, to create a position from which they would be able to move further forward. Anton says it was an idiotic plan: there was no difference whether you had to run 250 or 500 meters, after 30 seconds in an open area you would be a “toast”. The commander began sending groups of 5: on the first day, 4 groups were sent, all 20 ended up dead. No one could even reach that tank. The next day another 20 people got killed. Anton says, Ukrainians have 15–20 various drones — both killer drones and reconnaissance drones — in the air at any time, day or night. The drones see any movement immediately. “It felt like the Ukrainian Armed Forces had a 50-fold advantage in drones,” he says. Then the commanders decided to send only 2 people at once. One group managed to reach the tank and dug in, and the propagandists on TV immediately began reporting that “the village was taken.” But the Russian troops still haven’t even reached it. The commander, a former security guard from a supermarket, dreamed of seeing himself on Channel 1, to feel like a hero warrior. So, he kept sending one group after the other to the slaughter, demanding that they move forward towards the village. The group that dug in near the tank managed to survive, but they needed ammunition, food, water — so, more people were sent in to deliver supplies, and they kept being shot by the Ukrainian fire. Anton says that about 70 people died there in a week, near that tank. Anton says that the worst wasn’t even the gunfire — the worst was when you leave the dugout and are completely exposed, and you realize that at any second you can be killed. “I went out to the toilet, went back 30 seconds later, and at the place where I was, 2 mortars hit” he recalls. Sometimes the Ukrainian drone operators made errors and the drones fell down, then the commanders sent Russian soldiers into the minefields to pick them up. A task from which one is unlikely to return, because no one has maps of the minefields, the mines are just thrown in, where it falls, that’s where it falls. “You have a patch of land, 4 drones fly around it. They drop something, as soon as they fly away — the next 4 are already flying. And in the distance, there are probably 5 more, coordinating fire by mortars and artillery,” explains Anton. If a drone noticed you, you aren’t allowed to hide back in a dugout — because the operator sees a glowing dot, and suddenly it disappears: it means the person has gone somewhere. Then a precise hit arrives — and minimum 5 people in the dugout will be dead. Anton says that in 2 weeks, only 15–20 people were left from 250 soldiers that arrived, and from them 10 people were the commanders and non-combat clerks. Most of the soldiers were contractors, only a few were “mobilized”. From the losses, about 40% are dead, the rest are wounded. About 50% of the wounded are without legs or arms — disabled for life. “When I arrived, that village was still more or less intact. 3 weeks later it was just ruins. Heaps of corpses…” recalls Anton. He survived because he was part of the “evacuation team” — and he refused to go in the assaults, saying he would continue performing the task he was assigned to do. He was still going to the position near the tank, but his job was to pull the wounded, not carry provisions or stay in the dugout. Although Anton didn’t do any specific medical training, he had to perform an amputation in the field. This was like a horror movie. He pulled a guy who was lying wounded in the field for 3 days. The guy managed to apply tourniquets to wounds on his arm and leg, but after these 3 days his arm began to rot. The medics told him on the radio he had to amputate the arm. Anton injected the guy with all sedatives he could find and chopped the arm with an axe. It took him 4 attempts to get through the flesh and bones, then he had to treat the stump and bandage it. “I didn't sleep for two days after that,” Anton says. “When we were loading him [for evacuation], he was still alive, and he also made it to the first line alive. I don't know what happened to him after that.” Another guy that Anton pulled out had part of his jaw torn off, his arm up to the shoulder and half a leg. The commander was pissed off about it: "I don't need this, now I have to do something for one more person." A day later the injured guy was already begging to die, realizing he wouldn’t survive. At the end, he bled to death. The dead were rarely pulled out from the field. It was too much trouble to even attempt it. Once Anton had to hide from a drone and crawled into an old dugout, and realized he was crawling on top of liquified bodies in uniform. The bodies were there for already 3–4 months. There was one guy in the unit of about 18–19, he was a draftee (all Russian men have to serve a 1-year compulsory military service, but the draftees are not supposed to be sent to Ukraine to the war). That guy was also tricked into signing a contract — in the military enlistment office where he arrived as a draftee, they simply gave him some papers to sign, and he signed, not realizing what it was. “A week and a half later, he was already at the front line,” says Anton. The guy’s family sent a letter, complaining to the prosecutor's office that he was forced to sign the contract. The battalion commander was furious about it and gave the order to “sort him out.” The teenage soldier was sent into an attack and killed within a week. Anton says his commander was constantly drunk. One day the commander ordered him to pick another drone from the headquarters — Anton argued it was unnecessary to do it at night, as they had a spare drone they could use, and at night it’s really easy to see a person on thermal visors. But the commander insisted. Anton managed to get to the headquarters, where they gave him a drone and a package “for the commander”. Anton looked inside the bag, and there were bottles of vodka and cognac. The commander sent him to get the alcohol for him and he didn’t care it was deadly dangerous. On the way back, Anton heard a drone over him and immediately an explosive dropped on him. Anton was wounded and couldn’t walk, but he realized he still had both his arms and legs. He threw away the bag with vodka and crawled into the nearest basement, got on the radio, said that he was wounded and asked for evacuation. They responded it was too dangerous to try to get him. After 20 minutes, he realized that he was bleeding out. “I was shaking all over, tremors, I definitely lost a liter of blood,” says Anton. He decided to crawl, and managed to make it to the line where he could be picked up — out of the firing range. Anton says that ”almost everyone drinks” at the front line — or they are using cheap drugs (“salts”). The commanders also steal strong pain killers from the first aid kits given to soldiers and use those. If a soldier refuses to follow orders, he isn’t sent to a military court for prosecution but simply shot by the commander’s underlings — his arms and legs are taped to a tree, and he’s shot at a point blank range. Sometimes a person may be dressed in 2 bulletproof vests and then shot at with a machine gun, his ribs get broken and he slowly dies. Or he’s shot at through a helmet — such shots take off the whole skull. Anton says that 2 soldiers in his unit were liquidated like this, for not following orders — they refused to go in an attack, because all previous groups were killed. Anton himself nearly got shot — when in the field, he noticed a drone in the sky and went back, but took to the left and ended up in a neighboring unit. That unit was looking for a mobilized soldier on the run and took Anton for the deserter. He was tied to a tree and about to be shot, there was a hole nearby, where 20–30 bodies were already lying. He was saved by a radio message that the runaway soldier was found. Do the Russian soldiers realize that Russia’s war in Ukraine is evil? Do they blame Putin for that? Nobody among the Russian troops at the front says things like "let's go overthrow Putin,” states Anton. “Of course, they say that he [Putin] has started some kind of screwup that no one needs.” ”Even the ‘patriots’ when they arrive, very soon start saying, ‘What are we even doing here, why the heck do we need this?’” “There are some ‘ultra patriots’, but they do not survive for long, because they are the first to run ahead and the first to get killed.” “There was this guy, 54 years old, his wife had cancer. He came not even for the money, but because he needed the benefits for a serviceman's family, so his wife could get the cancer treatment. He was saying: ‘I know that people get killed here, I made my choice. If I get killed, at least my wife will get 5 million ruble, she will get the treatment, the children will live well." That guy lived in a small regional town. His monthly salary was 35,000 ruble (about USD$400). He had 3 kids, his wife was sick. He saw it as his only option to help the wife and the kids. “You are not a human being there at all,” says Anton. He fears what is going to happen in Russia when all these people with the broken psyche come back. “When these people come back from the war with blood on their hands, with a broken psyche, who were in the same companies, detachments and so on, they will start to form groups, and these smaller groups will start to form bigger groups...” Anton says that plenty of weapons are transported back to Russia in bags with dead bodies — pulled into parts and hidden in these bags. An AK-47 costs about 40,000 ruble in Russia now ($460). Anton says that if the Russian soldiers are being utilized at the same rate as at his part of the front, Russia has suffered about 400,000 losses by now — killed and badly wounded. Anton says that no one signing an army contract should hope they’d come back with the money — because they won’t. At best, they can hope to come back home with the money in case of a serious wound — but then, “Do you want your mother to be wiping off your butt for the rest of your life?” “If you think there are some Nazis there... There are no Nazis, there are ordinary people. If you, so to say, go and kill your neighbor, would you be able to live with that for the rest of your life?” “This war is not worth it. This is not a war for the Fatherland, this is not a war for justice, not a war for freedom — this is a war for the complete bullshit. A war for the grandfather who is so crazy that he went and killed hundreds of thousands of people for nothing, just like that.” “You are not liberating anyone. He [the crazy grandfather] himself doesn't believe that he is liberating anyone, he doesn't give a f**k about all this — and even less about you.” What can the Russian men do to avoid being sent to the war? “Better run,” says Anton. ”No money? Take out loans and use that money to escape.” Anton himself deserted after getting wounded. Yesterday, Putin signed a decree raising the federal payout on signing the army contact to 400,000 rub. ($4,600) — it’s nearly twice as much as the state was paying before. Regions are also raising their payouts — St. Petersburg just raised it’s top-up to 1.8 million, and Moscow already lifted it to 1.9 million rub. ($22,000). Russia is running out of volunteers, so the prices for cannon fodder are rising. Putin is too scared to do another mobilization and force people to kill and die, because he knows how unpopular this war really is.

What do you think of the statement by Vladimir Putin that the events in Kursk Oblast were a "provocation" by Ukraine? Putin already upgraded his definition of events in the Kursk region of Russia from “a provocation” to “a situation”. The Ukrainian side remains tight-lipped on “the situation” in Kursk, while the Russian media tries to downplay the breakthrough at the border by the Ukrainian troops. Every evening Russian propagandists report that “the Ukrainian troops have been destroyed” — and the next morning we find out that the Ukrainians have moved forward another 10–15 km and took several more settlements. What the Russian military correspondents have reported: Russian oppositional media gives a slightly different map, where already 700 square km are under control of the Ukrainian Armed Forces. One notable point about the Ukrainian operation in the Kursk region is that the local population is completely passive. When Russian tanks invaded the Ukrainian soil in February 2022, locals threw Molotov cocktails at them and burned them, tried to stop tanks with bare hands by simply standing in front, people blocked the Russian military equipment and went to rallies with Ukrainian flags. But there is no resistance from the Russian local population. In the town of Sudzha, the Ukrainian forces surrounded the police station and the cops simply put their hands up without resisting. Ukrainians took their weapons away and let them go. The ones who wanted to leave the town were allowed to leave for Kursk. This morning, the news came that the border in the Belgorod region has also been broken through by the Ukrainian troops that took over a village in 3 km from the border. Bryansk region is next.

What is the most likely path for the Ukrainian Armed Forces into the Russian territory starting in the Kursk region? Why? The most likely path for the Ukrainian armed forces into the Kursk region is where the Russian troops aren’t present — or where the commanders choose not to resist. There are basically no “contract troops” in the Kursk region, only the units made of regular draftees — 18–19-year-old boys serving the compulsory 1-year term. These troops have been abandoned for 4 days, without communication from their superiors, with no food or water. The commanders told them to “stay there”, but draftees aren’t supposed to be used in combat. 5-million ruble death payouts are reserved only for the troops that are located in “the area of SMO” — on occupied Ukrainian territories. The troops located in the Kursk region aren’t in the war zone and won’t be paid for getting wounded or killed. They are also not getting paid 200,000 rub. ($2,400) per month in wages. So, many Russian commanders choose to surrender with their “bunch of teens in uniforms” as opposed to trying to fight against the experienced, combat-hardened Ukrainian units. Reportedly, small groups of the Ukrainian forces moved as far as 45 km in depth at some directions, towards strategic targets. They avoid battles and move forward where it’s easier to get through. And the main group of Ukrainian forces is moving steadily with all the logistics after them, clearing the islands of resistance of scattered Russian units. Captured Russian soldiers. Apparently, over 300 Russian soldiers have already surrendered, creating a logistical problem for tie Ukrainians — transport is required to take them to the Ukrainian territory, but trucks and cars are needed to support the offensive. Commander of the Ukrainian Armed Forces Syrskyi posted this photo from “the area near the offensive operations”. The Ukrainian commanders have a plan — I’d say, they have several plans — and they are following the path that’s the most advantageous in the current situation. And no one, except them, knows what is the overall plan. Let’s wait and see.

Isn't it delusional to think that Putin is planning to recreate the Soviet Empire and conquer Eastern Europe? Does Putin have the military capability to accomplish such endeavors? By now, it’s apparent to anyone with the ability to think rationally, that Vladimir Putin is delusional and his plan to recreate the USSR has utterly failed — but Vladimir Putin isn’t rational. Vladimir Putin is a sadistic murderer and deluded megalomaniac. In his delusion, he’s a messiah whose job is to destroy “the evil West” — the USA and the European Union — and restore “traditional values”. And he’s the only one who can do the job. His conviction in his own status as “the chosen one” was confirmed (in his eyes) by his unbelievable rise from an average KGB clerk to the ruler of the largest country in the world. Shamans, clairvoyants and magicians — Putin believes in supernatural things and his buddies indulged him by bringing thoroughly prepped fraudsters for secret meetings with the self-proclaimed “tsar of the whole Rus” — and these “shamans” convinced Putin that’s it was the Creator’s plan and he must fulfill it: make Russia great again. So, anyone trying to talk to Putin rationally is doomed. It’s like trying to convince a schizophrenic that “the voices” talking to him aren’t real. For him, the voices are the most real thing in the world.

Can Ukraine make its own weapons? Ukraine can and does make its own weapons: Russia-Ukraine war of 2022–2024 is the first war in history where drones became the weapons that dominate the terrain. Within the last 2 years, drone production in Ukraine grew 100-fold. Since February 2022, Ukraine created and developed the UAV market from the ground up. One of such manufacturers are making drones called “Hornets”. There are smaller and larger FPV drones — “Wild Hornets”, “Queen Hornets”, as well as other models. All of them are Ukrainian-made. The Ukrainian drone operators have learned to use the same drone for many missions — a drone drops explosives and returns to the base, to get munitions. Drones are even used to retrieve weapons from the battlefield. Here you can see “Hornet Queen” picking weapons on the battlefield using a magnet. In December 2023, Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy set the task of producing a million drones for the Ukrainian Armed Forces. By now, the task has been completed, says Ukraine’s minister of digital transformation Mykhailo Fedorov. There are already contracts for the production of a million of drones for the Ukrainian army. They include standard FPV drones, long-range, reconnaissance and other types of drones that are already used by the Ukrainian defenders at the front. Just imagine this number: 1,000,000 drones! It’s 2 drones per each Russian soldier on the Ukrainian land. But tens of thousands of drones go directly from manufacturers to the Ukrainian units at the front without involving the government and the ministry of defense. They are paid for from donations that people make on behalf of certain units. So, if a certain unit requires more drones, they place a request with a manufacturer they know, and get a delivery within days, without the need for ministerial approvals. This is why the Ukrainian army is so much more efficient, and why the Russian soldiers say that it feels like the Ukrainians have 50:1 advantage in drones. This also saves thousands of Ukrainian lives.

Do you think Sergei Lavrov can be president of the United Nations? Russia is presiding over the 15-member Security Council of the United Nations this month. In an Orwellian twist, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov (who is sanctioned by the EU and the U.S.) was allowed to fly to New York City to take over the presidency in the UNSC. Of course, Lavrov used the Security Council presidency to push Russia’s anti-Ukrainian agenda. In 1939, the same sentiment was used by another “savior”: “Germany cannot watch indifferently as Danzig is destroyed and everything German is oppressed,” proclaimed Adolf H. on September 1. Barbara Woodward, the UK Representative at the Security Council, gave a perfect response to Lavrov’s allegations. “President [Lavrov] while you tell us how you believe the world order can become more just, democratic and sustainable, your military is systematically bombing civilians in Ukraine in an unprovoked war of aggression and in flagrant violation of the UN Charter. What is just about trying to annex another country’s land? What is democratic about trying to subjugate another country’s people? What is sustainable about waging a war that has killed or injured over 500,000 of your own people? The war in Ukraine is a stark reminder of what kind of world order Russia really wants – a world where might is right, and powerful countries can bully and invade other countries with impunity. The UK does not accept such a world. We will continue to stand staunchly behind Ukraine. We will support its aspiration for a just and lasting peace in line with the UN Charter and international law, and its demand for accountability. We will continue to be a tireless advocate for effective multilateralism and for the principles at the heart of the UN Charter,” Woodward concluded. Lavrov might be a president of the UNSC this month. But he’s not getting a smooth ride.

If Vladimir Putin learned he only had a few weeks to live, would he nuke the USA? Absolutely not: Vladimir Putin is a paranoidal sadist, but he’s certainly not seeking to destroy his life’s work and die a terrible death. If anything, he’s “a family man” and since recently have been bringing his 2 official daughters, a niece and a nephew closer, appointing them into the most important for him positions of power. He also has grandkids and spoke lovingly about them in the past. Since recently, Putin brought his daughters Maria and Katerina into the limelight. More than anything, a tale-telling sign is that Kremlin bots hysterically scream that “Putin will press the button if he is in a desperate situation.” There are more facts that point to Putin’s not being in a position to order a nuclear strike on the USA: Remember, Putin lives in isolation from the real world. Cubans handed in their treasures to be able to own a TV, which fed them more propaganda. In 1991, the USSR collapsed and the Soviets left Cuba. But another benefactor arrived in no time: China brought its Haier refrigerators, along with pots and pans — the only problem here, not much food to cook and refrigerate. The hope for a miracle rejuvenated, maybe the Chinese would help to fix Cuba’s economic disaster? When this didn’t eventuate either, Fidel Castro decided to allow private entrepreneurship, and people again had high hopes, began brainstorming ideas and business plans. Cubans began buying and selling stuff, investing, borrowing. Until the regime changed its mind and began taking away business licenses and banning whole sectors, like 3D cinemas, just like that. No apologies or compensations. Then Obama became the president of the USA, and Cubans again began hoping that things would get better — that the Americans would finally "invade" Cuba with their yachts, cars, and cruise ships, leaving bigs tips and showering locals with cash. These hopes crashed as well. Then Russia 2.0 arrived. And once again, Cubans were hoping that things would finally change, that this time they for sure would get out of poverty and misery. They were assured that this time there were real plans, projects and opportunities for everyone. Cubans forgot that the former USSR had been investing in Cuba 4 billion dollars per year, for 30 years. Nothing changed before, so why would things be different this time? Food shortages and energy blackouts are acute in Cuba. “No bread or milk, many kids don’t have breakfast, blackouts last 10+ hours per day.” The Castro regime stripped people of their dignity and made them dependent on its injustices. The worse they are treated by the regime, the more they defend it, because they need these crumbs. Socialism and communism are the cancer of the world.

Why is Orban so pro-Russian? Bottom photo: Miklos Horthy, regent of the Kingdom of Hungary in 1920-1944 with Adolf Hitler. Top photo: Vladimir Putin with Victor Orbán, prime minister of Hungary since 2010. After an unannounced visit to Kyiv to meet president Zelenskyy on July 2, Orbán “suddenly” decided to fly to Moscow on July 5 for personal talks with Vladimir Putin. Kremlin’s speaker Dmitry Peskov denied that Orbán’s visit was planned before the Hungarian president went to meet with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, and insisted that Orbán’s request to visit Moscow only arrived on July 3. (And we know what it means when Peskov is denying something.) In the meeting with Orbán, Putin repeated his ridiculous ultimatum for Ukraine to surrender 4 regions (within their administrative boundaries) to Russia, which he first verbalized in mid-June, days before the Swiss Global Peace Summit, organized by Ukraine. Surely, for Orbán it was a shock, because just a day before in Astana (Kazakhstan), Putin was saying that Russia would be happy with the outline of the preliminary draft agreement achieved between the Russian and Ukrainian delegations in March 2022 in Istanbul, which had absolutely different conditions. What could be the reason for Putin’s sudden “change of heart”? Maybe 2 or more reasons are correct. For starters, Putin said that he was talking to Orbán as the chairman of the European Union — the formal position that Hungary took from July 1 — and Putin’s ridiculous ultimatum was to the EU. Obviouslty, Orbán had no authority from the EU to negotiate with Putin — he was too chicken to even inform the EU that he was flying to Moscow. When the news about the visit spread, Polish leader asked Orbán in disbelief if it were true. So, Putin used Orbán like a pawn, luring him to Moscow with a prospect of becoming a “peacemaker” — and then sacrificing him to paint a picture for his serfs, positioning himself as a victorious leader who is visited by the chairman of the EU begging to stop the war. Not only Orbán was unsuccessful in convincing Zelenskyy to announce a ceasefire, but he was treated by Putin as a whipping boy, allowing the Kremlin tyrant to elevate his own status among the local patriots and lift the spirits of Russian soldiers, who only want to get back home alive. Which of course wouldn’t be happening if Putin’s situation was advantageous and he had good prospects. Putin is facing a bottomless abyss, and that’s the only reason he keeps asking for “peace” — which Russians could have any day if they simply withdrew their troops from Ukraine. But Putin never wanted peace — if he did, he would have never invaded. Putin wants his troops to have carte blanche to do whatever they wish on the occupied Ukrainian territories — and do it with impunity. Putin needs to present a victory to the Russian population that’s growing increasingly tired of the war and angry about their own worsening situation. Putin needs to save the Russian economy from collapse, and for the western sanctions to be lifted, before Russia turns into a cold-climate version of North Korea. P.S. Orban left just hours before Hurricane Orkhan hit the Russian capital. A fateful omen.

Now the real success speaks for itself: our active defensive actions on the other side of the border and Putin’s inability to protect his territory from our defensive actions of this kind are very telling." Truth is, most likely the Ukrainians kept quiet about the plan to invade Russia because they had experience of their plans leaked to Russians. One of previous operations was reportedly cancelled because Russians found out about the plan, and the big offensive of 2023 didn’t turn out well for Ukraine because Russians knew where the Ukrainian forces planned to attack. Apparently, only commander-in-chief Syrskyi and president Zelenskyy himself, along with a few top generals, knew about the plan. Even the people in the office of the Ukrainian president didn’t know: Syrskyi talked to Zelenskyy 1-to-1. The Main Intelligence Directorate (GUR) didn’t participate in planning the Kursk operation; the army used its own intel. The soldiers of the Ukrainian forces found out about the operation just hours before. In the briefing for foreign diplomates, Zelenskyy explained that right now a huge ideological change is occurring: "The whole naive illusory concept of Russia’s so-called ‘red lines’, which prevailed in some partners’ assessment of the war, crumbled somewhere near Sudzha over these few days." “Now the world sees that it is realistic, that it really works. Not only in the temporarily occupied territory of our country but in the territory of Russia as well. The world sees that everything in this war depends only on courage — our courage, and the courage of our partners,” said Zelenskyy. All we need is courage. And weapons.
